glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Through washing, clothing, anointing, sacrifice, and a sacred meal, Aaron and his sons are consecrated as priests and the altar is made most holy, and the LORD declares the purpose behind it all: He brought Israel out of Egypt so that He might dwell among them.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Exodus 29 follows the description of the priestly garments in chapter 28. Moses receives the instructions on Sinai, and they are carried out later, in Leviticus 8–9.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Exodus 29:1–9 — Aaron and His Sons Are Washed, Clothed, and Anointed

  • Exodus 29:10–18 — The Sin Offering and the Burnt Offering

  • Exodus 29:19–28 — The Ram of Consecration and the Priests’ Portion

  • Exodus 29:29–37 — The Consecration Meal and Seven Days of Atonement for the Altar

  • Exodus 29:38–46 — The Continual Offering and the LORD’s Dwelling Among Israel

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “And they shall know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them up out of the land of Egypt, that I may dwell among them. I am the LORD their God.” (Exodus 29:46)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Priests who will stand between a holy God and His people must themselves be made fit to serve. The ceremony moves step by step. Aaron and his sons are washed at the door of the tabernacle, clothed in their holy garments, and Aaron is anointed with oil. Then come the sacrifices. They lay their hands on a bull as a sin offering, because the priests themselves need atonement before they can serve. A ram is burned whole as an offering of complete dedication. With the second ram, blood is put on the priests’ right ear, right thumb, and right big toe, setting apart what they hear, what they do, and where they walk. For seven days the consecration continues, and the altar itself is made most holy.

The chapter ends by lifting its eyes from details to purpose. Every morning and every evening a lamb is offered at the door of the tent, “where I will meet you to speak with you” (29:42). Then God says why He did everything: “I will dwell among the children of Israel and will be their God” (29:45). He brought them out of Egypt “that I may dwell among them” (29:46). The exodus, the covenant, the tabernacle, and the priesthood all serve that one goal.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Exodus 29:1–9 — Aaron and His Sons Are Washed, Clothed, and Anointed

Moses is to bring a young bull, two rams, and unleavened bread, then wash Aaron and his sons at the door of the tabernacle and dress them in their holy garments. He anoints Aaron with oil, and the priesthood becomes theirs by a lasting statute.

Exodus 29:10–18 — The Sin Offering and the Burnt Offering

Aaron and his sons lay their hands on a bull, whose blood is put on the altar’s horns and whose body is burned outside the camp as a sin offering. They lay their hands on the first ram, which is burned whole on the altar as a pleasing burnt offering to the LORD.

Exodus 29:19–28 — The Ram of Consecration and the Priests’ Portion

Blood from the second ram is put on the right ear, thumb, and big toe of Aaron and his sons, and blood and anointing oil are sprinkled on them and their garments to set them apart. Portions of the ram and bread are waved before the LORD and burned, and the breast and thigh become the priests’ lasting share of Israel’s peace offerings.

Exodus 29:29–37 — The Consecration Meal and Seven Days of Atonement for the Altar

Aaron’s garments are to pass to his sons, and the priests eat the ram and bread by which their atonement was made, food no outsider may eat. The consecration lasts seven days, with a bull offered daily to atone for the altar until it becomes most holy.

Exodus 29:38–46 — The Continual Offering and the LORD’s Dwelling Among Israel

Two lambs are offered every day, one in the morning and one at twilight, at the door of the tabernacle, where the LORD will meet with Israel and make the place holy by His glory. He declares that He will dwell among them and be their God, for this is why He brought them out of Egypt.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Exodus 29 states the goal of the whole book in God’s own words: He redeemed Israel so that He could live among them. That purpose runs from the garden to the Word who “dwelt among us” (John 1:14) and on to the new creation, where God dwells with His people forever (Revelation 21:3).

The chapter also shows how much it took for sinners to serve a holy God. Aaron needed a sin offering for himself, and the sacrifices had to be repeated morning and evening. Hebrews points to the difference in Jesus, a High Priest who needed no offering for His own sins and offered Himself once for all (Hebrews 7:26–28). In union with Him, His people are set apart to offer themselves to God.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Consecration for service. Washing, clothing, anointing, and sacrifice set the priests apart (29:1–9, 19–21).

Atonement before ministry. The priests and the altar need atonement before they can serve (29:10–14, 33, 36–37).

The whole person set apart. Blood on ear, thumb, and toe dedicates what the priest hears, does, and where he walks (29:20).

Continual worship. A lamb is offered every morning and evening (29:38–42).

God dwelling among His people. The LORD brought Israel out of Egypt so that He might dwell among them (29:45–46).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Consecrate (29:1, 9). To set apart as holy for God’s service. The ceremony consecrates the priests and the altar.

Sin offering (29:14). A sacrifice that dealt with sin. Its body was burned outside the camp.

Ram of consecration (29:22). The second ram, whose blood was applied to the priests and whose meat they ate as part of their setting apart.

Wave offering (29:24). A portion lifted and moved before the LORD to present it to Him.

Continual burnt offering (29:42). The lamb offered every morning and evening at the door of the tabernacle.

focus: Exodus 29 sets out the seven-day ceremony by which Aaron and his sons are washed, clothed, anointed, and consecrated as priests, and the altar is made most holy. The chapter closes with the continual morning and evening offering at the door of the tabernacle of meeting, where the LORD will meet His people, and with the LORD’s own statement of why He brought Israel out of Egypt: “that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 29:46).

sections.title: Aaron and His Sons Are Washed, Clothed, and Anointed
sections.summary: Moses is to bring a young bull, two rams, and unleavened bread, then wash Aaron and his sons at the door of the tabernacle of meeting and clothe them in their holy garments. He is to pour the anointing oil on Aaron’s head, and “The priesthood shall be theirs for a perpetual statute” (Exodus 29:9).

sections.title: The Sin Offering and the Burnt Offering
sections.summary: Aaron and his sons lay their hands on the bull, whose blood is put on the horns of the altar and whose flesh is burned outside the camp as a sin offering. They lay their hands on the first ram, which is burned whole on the altar as a burnt offering, “a sweet aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD” (Exodus 29:18).

sections.title: The Ram of Consecration and the Priests’ Portion
sections.summary: The blood of the second ram is put on the right ear, thumb, and big toe of Aaron and his sons, and blood and anointing oil are sprinkled on them and their garments so that they are hallowed. Portions of the ram and the bread are waved before the LORD and burned, and the breast and thigh become the priests’ portion from Israel’s peace offerings by a statute forever.

sections.title: The Consecration Meal and Seven Days of Atonement for the Altar
sections.summary: Aaron’s holy garments are to pass to his sons, and Aaron and his sons eat the ram and bread “with which the atonement was made” (Exodus 29:33), which no outsider may eat. For seven days they are consecrated, and a bull is offered each day to atone for the altar until “the altar shall be most holy” (Exodus 29:37).

sections.title: The Continual Offering and the LORD’s Dwelling Among Israel
sections.summary: Two lambs are offered every day, one in the morning and one at twilight, as a continual burnt offering at the door of the tabernacle of meeting, where the LORD will meet with Israel and sanctify the tabernacle by His glory. He declares, “I will dwell among the children of Israel and will be their God” (Exodus 29:45), for He brought them out of Egypt “that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 29:46).

1.brief: To hallow Aaron and his sons for the priesthood, Moses is to take one young bull and two rams without blemish. The consecration begins with the sacrifices God requires.
1.explain:
“And this is what you shall do to them to hallow them for ministering to Me as priests:”

God now describes the ceremony that will “hallow” Aaron and his sons, setting them apart as holy for priestly service. Leviticus 8 records the ceremony carried out.

“Take one young bull and two rams without blemish,”

Three animals are needed, all “without blemish.” Each has its own part in the ceremony (29:10–28).

2.brief: Moses is to prepare unleavened bread, cakes mixed with oil, and wafers anointed with oil, made of wheat flour. Bread offerings accompany the animal sacrifices.
2.explain:
“and unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil (you shall make them of wheat flour).”

Three kinds of unleavened bread are prepared from “wheat flour,” some with oil. Bread offerings accompany the animal sacrifices.

3.brief: The breads are put in one basket and brought with the bull and two rams. Everything needed for the ceremony is gathered together.
3.explain:
“You shall put them in one basket and bring them in the basket, with the bull and the two rams.”

The breads are placed in “one basket.” Everything needed for the ceremony is gathered together.

4.brief: Aaron and his sons are brought to the door of the tabernacle of meeting and washed with water. Cleansing comes first in preparing them to serve.
4.explain:
“And Aaron and his sons you shall bring to the door of the tabernacle of meeting,”

The priests are brought to the entrance of the tent.

“and you shall wash them with water.”

Moses washes them. Cleansing comes first in preparing them to serve.
4.notes: The later laver at the tent was for the priests’ daily washing of hands and feet (30:17–21). This washing at their consecration was a full cleansing.

5.brief: Moses puts the tunic, robe, ephod, and breastplate on Aaron and girds him with the woven band. Aaron is clothed in the garments God designed.
5.explain:
“Then you shall take the garments, put the tunic on Aaron, and the robe of the ephod, the ephod, and the breastplate,”

Moses dresses Aaron in the garments described in chapter 28, layer by layer.

“and gird him with the intricately woven band of the ephod.”

The band ties the ephod in place. Aaron is clothed in the garments God designed.

6.brief: The turban is put on Aaron’s head, with the holy crown on the turban. The high priest’s headdress marks him as set apart to God.
6.explain:
“You shall put the turban on his head, and put the holy crown on the turban.”

“The holy crown” is the gold plate engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD (28:36–37; 39:30). The high priest’s headdress marks him as set apart to God.

7.brief: Moses pours the anointing oil on Aaron’s head and anoints him. The anointing sets Aaron apart for his office.
7.explain:
“And you shall take the anointing oil, pour it on his head, and anoint him.”

The oil is poured “on his head.” The anointing sets Aaron apart for his office. Psalm 133:2 pictures the oil running down Aaron’s beard to the edge of his garments. Aaron’s anointing points ahead to Jesus, the Anointed One, who was anointed with the Spirit (Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38).
7.notes: The title Messiah comes from the Hebrew word for anointed, and Christ from its Greek equivalent.

8.brief: Aaron’s sons are brought and clothed in tunics. The other priests are clothed in turn.
8.explain:
“Then you shall bring his sons and put tunics on them.”

Aaron’s sons are clothed next. The other priests are clothed in turn.

9.brief: Aaron and his sons are girded with sashes and given hats, and “The priesthood shall be theirs for a perpetual statute.” God establishes a lasting priesthood in Aaron’s family.
9.explain:
“And you shall gird them with sashes, Aaron and his sons, and put the hats on them.”

Sashes and hats complete their garments.

“The priesthood shall be theirs for a perpetual statute. So you shall consecrate Aaron and his sons.”

The priesthood belongs to Aaron’s family “for a perpetual statute.” God establishes a lasting priesthood in Aaron’s line.

10.brief: The bull is brought before the tabernacle, and Aaron and his sons lay their hands on its head. By laying on hands they identify themselves with the sacrifice.
10.explain:
“You shall also have the bull brought before the tabernacle of meeting,”

The first sacrifice is the bull.

“and Aaron and his sons shall put their hands on the head of the bull.”

The priests “put their hands” on its head. By laying on hands they identify themselves with the sacrifice, which will die in connection with their sin.

11.brief: The bull is killed before the LORD at the door of the tabernacle. The sacrifice is made in God’s presence.
11.explain:
“Then you shall kill the bull before the LORD, by the door of the tabernacle of meeting.”

The bull is killed “before the LORD.” The sacrifice is made in God’s presence.

12.brief: Some of the bull’s blood is put on the horns of the altar, and the rest is poured at its base. The blood is applied to the altar as part of the cleansing.
12.explain:
“You shall take some of the blood of the bull and put it on the horns of the altar with your finger,”

Moses puts blood “on the horns of the altar.”

“and pour all the blood beside the base of the altar.”

The rest is poured out at the base. The blood is applied to the altar as part of its cleansing (29:36).

13.brief: The fat, the fatty lobe of the liver, and the kidneys are burned on the altar. The choicest parts are given to God.
13.explain:
“And you shall take all the fat that covers the entrails, the fatty lobe attached to the liver, and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, and burn them on the altar.”

The fat and certain organs are burned on the altar. The fat was regarded as the choicest part and belonged to God (Leviticus 3:16).

14.brief: The bull’s flesh, skin, and offal are burned outside the camp, for “It is a sin offering.” The priests themselves need atonement for sin before they can serve, a contrast Hebrews 7:27 draws with Christ.
14.explain:
“But the flesh of the bull, with its skin and its offal, you shall burn with fire outside the camp.”

The rest of the bull is burned “outside the camp.” The priests did not eat it.

“It is a sin offering.”

The bull is a sin offering. Aaron and his sons, about to serve as priests, first needed atonement for their own sin. Hebrews 7:26–27 contrasts Christ, who is “holy, harmless, undefiled,” and does not need “to offer up sacrifices, first for His own sins.” Hebrews 13:11–12 notes that the bodies of sin offerings were burned outside the camp, and that Jesus “suffered outside the gate.”

15.brief: Aaron and his sons lay their hands on the first ram. The second sacrifice begins the same way.
15.explain:
“You shall also take one ram, and Aaron and his sons shall put their hands on the head of the ram;”

The second sacrifice is the first ram. The priests again lay their hands on it.

16.brief: The ram is killed, and its blood is sprinkled all around the altar. The blood marks the altar again.
16.explain:
“and you shall kill the ram, and you shall take its blood and sprinkle it all around on the altar.”

Its blood is sprinkled around the altar.

17.brief: The ram is cut in pieces, and its entrails and legs are washed and placed with the pieces and the head. The offering is prepared with care.
17.explain:
“Then you shall cut the ram in pieces, wash its entrails and its legs, and put them with its pieces and with its head.”

The ram is cut up, cleaned, and arranged. The offering is prepared with care.

18.brief: The whole ram is burned on the altar, “a sweet aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.” The burnt offering expresses full dedication to God.
18.explain:
“And you shall burn the whole ram on the altar.”

The whole ram is burned. Nothing is kept back.

“It is a burnt offering to the LORD; it is a sweet aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.”

This is “a burnt offering,” given entirely to God. It is “a sweet aroma,” pleasing to Him. The burnt offering expresses full dedication to God.

19.brief: Aaron and his sons lay their hands on the second ram. The ram of consecration is now prepared.
19.explain:
“You shall also take the other ram, and Aaron and his sons shall put their hands on the head of the ram.”

The third sacrifice is “the other ram,” called the ram of consecration (29:22).

20.brief: Some of its blood is put on the tip of the right ear, the thumb of the right hand, and the big toe of the right foot of Aaron and his sons, and the rest is sprinkled on the altar. Marking ear, hand, and foot sets apart the whole person of each priest for God’s service.
20.explain:
“Then you shall kill the ram, and take some of its blood and put it on the tip of the right ear of Aaron and on the tip of the right ear of his sons,”

Blood is put on “the tip of the right ear.”

“on the thumb of their right hand and on the big toe of their right foot,”

It is also put on the right “thumb” and right “big toe.” Ear, hand, and foot are marked. The priest must hear God’s word, do God’s work, and walk in God’s ways. Marking ear, hand, and foot sets apart the whole person of each priest for God’s service.

“and sprinkle the blood all around on the altar.”

The rest of the blood is sprinkled around the altar.
20.notes: The same rite was used in cleansing a healed leper (Leviticus 14:14, 25).

21.brief: Blood from the altar and anointing oil are sprinkled on Aaron, his sons, and their garments, so they and their garments are hallowed. The priests and their clothing are set apart together.
21.explain:
“And you shall take some of the blood that is on the altar, and some of the anointing oil, and sprinkle it on Aaron and on his garments, on his sons and on the garments of his sons with him;”

Blood from the altar and anointing oil are sprinkled on the priests and their clothes.

“and he and his garments shall be hallowed, and his sons and his sons’ garments with him.”

They and their garments are “hallowed.” The priests and their clothing are set apart together. Blood and oil, sacrifice and anointing, belong together in their consecration.

22.brief: Moses takes the fat, the fat tail, the inner fat, the liver lobe, the kidneys, and the right thigh, “for it is a ram of consecration.” These parts are set apart for the consecration offering.
22.explain:
“Also you shall take the fat of the ram, the fat tail, the fat that covers the entrails, the fatty lobe attached to the liver, the two kidneys and the fat on them, the right thigh”

Moses takes the fat portions and “the right thigh.”

“(for it is a ram of consecration),”

This is “a ram of consecration.” The Hebrew word is related to filling the hand, the expression for installing a priest (28:41). These parts are set apart for the consecration offering.

23.brief: One loaf, one cake made with oil, and one wafer are taken from the basket of unleavened bread before the LORD. The bread joins the offering.
23.explain:
“one loaf of bread, one cake made with oil, and one wafer from the basket of the unleavened bread that is before the LORD;”

One of each kind of bread is taken from the basket.

24.brief: Moses is to put all these portions in the hands of Aaron and his sons and wave them as a wave offering before the LORD. Moses presents the offering while the portions rest in the hands of the priests being consecrated.
24.explain:
“and you shall put all these in the hands of Aaron and in the hands of his sons,”

Moses puts the portions “in the hands” of the priests. Their hands are literally filled, the picture behind the word for consecration.

“and you shall wave them as a wave offering before the LORD.”

The offering is waved “before the LORD,” presented to Him. Moses presents the offering while the portions rest in the hands of the priests being consecrated.

25.brief: Moses takes the waved portions back from their hands and burns them on the altar as a burnt offering, a sweet aroma to the LORD. These portions go wholly to God, unlike the breast Moses receives in Exodus 29:26 and the meat Aaron and his sons eat in Exodus 29:32.
25.explain:
“You shall receive them back from their hands and burn them on the altar as a burnt offering,”

Moses takes the portions back and burns them on the altar.

“as a sweet aroma before the LORD. It is an offering made by fire to the LORD.”

These portions go wholly to God, “a sweet aroma before the LORD.”

26.brief: Moses waves the breast of the ram before the LORD, and it becomes his portion. Moses, who performs the consecration, receives a share.
26.explain:
“Then you shall take the breast of the ram of Aaron’s consecration and wave it as a wave offering before the LORD;”

Moses waves “the breast” of the ram before the LORD.

“and it shall be your portion.”

The breast is “your portion,” Moses’ share. At this consecration Moses acts as the priest who installs Aaron.

27.brief: The breast that is waved and the thigh that is raised are consecrated as the portion for Aaron and his sons. Unlike Moses’ portion of this ram in verse 26, this provision looks ahead to Israel’s future peace offerings, from which the priests will receive the breast and thigh by a lasting statute (verse 28).
27.explain:
“And from the ram of the consecration you shall consecrate the breast of the wave offering which is waved, and the thigh of the heave offering which is raised,”

The breast that is “waved” and the thigh that is “raised” are set apart.

“of that which is for Aaron and of that which is for his sons.”

In later peace offerings, these portions will belong to Aaron and his sons.

28.brief: The breast and thigh are to come from Israel’s peace offerings for Aaron and his sons as a statute forever. The people will provide for the priests who serve them.
28.explain:
“It shall be from the children of Israel for Aaron and his sons by a statute forever.”

The priests’ share will come “from the children of Israel.”

“For it is a heave offering; it shall be a heave offering from the children of Israel from the sacrifices of their peace offerings, that is, their heave offering to the LORD.”

When Israel brings “peace offerings,” the breast and thigh go to the priests (Leviticus 7:30–34). The people will provide for the priests who serve them.

29.brief: Aaron’s holy garments will pass to his sons after him, to be anointed and consecrated in them. The priesthood continues through the generations.
29.explain:
“And the holy garments of Aaron shall be his sons’ after him, to be anointed in them and to be consecrated in them.”

Aaron’s garments pass to his successors. The priesthood continues through the generations. Numbers 20:25–28 records Aaron’s garments placed on Eleazar.

30.brief: The son who becomes priest in Aaron’s place will wear them for seven days when he enters to minister. Each new high priest is consecrated in the same way.
30.explain:
“That son who becomes priest in his place shall put them on for seven days,”

Each new high priest wears the garments “for seven days.”

“when he enters the tabernacle of meeting to minister in the holy place.”

Each new high priest is consecrated in the same way.

31.brief: The ram of consecration is boiled in the holy place. The meal is prepared in a holy setting.
31.explain:
“And you shall take the ram of the consecration and boil its flesh in the holy place.”

The remaining meat of the ram is boiled “in the holy place,” the sacred area near the tent. The meal is prepared in a holy setting.

32.brief: Aaron and his sons eat the ram and the bread at the door of the tabernacle. The priests share a sacred meal at the entrance of God’s dwelling.
32.explain:
“Then Aaron and his sons shall eat the flesh of the ram, and the bread that is in the basket, by the door of the tabernacle of meeting.”

The priests eat the meat and bread “by the door of the tabernacle.” They share a sacred meal at the entrance of God’s dwelling. Fellowship with God follows sacrifice.

33.brief: Aaron and his sons eat the things by which atonement was made to consecrate them, but no outsider may eat them, “because they are holy.” The meal belongs only to those being set apart.
33.explain:
“They shall eat those things with which the atonement was made, to consecrate and to sanctify them;”

The priests eat the food “with which the atonement was made.”

“but an outsider shall not eat them, because they are holy.”

“An outsider,” anyone not of the priestly family, may not eat. The meal belongs only to those being set apart.

34.brief: Anything left until morning must be burned and not eaten, “because it is holy.” The holy food may not be treated as ordinary.
34.explain:
“And if any of the flesh of the consecration offerings, or of the bread, remains until the morning, then you shall burn the remainder with fire.”

If any of the meat or bread remains until morning, it must be burned and may not be eaten.

“It shall not be eaten, because it is holy.”

The holy food may not be treated as ordinary.

35.brief: Moses is to do all this for Aaron and his sons and consecrate them for seven days. The consecration lasts a full week.
35.explain:
“Thus you shall do to Aaron and his sons, according to all that I have commanded you.”

Moses must follow every instruction.

“Seven days you shall consecrate them.”

The consecration lasts “seven days,” a full week. Leviticus 8:33–35 records the priests staying at the tent throughout those days.

36.brief: A bull is offered every day as a sin offering for atonement, and the altar is cleansed, atoned for, and anointed to sanctify it. The altar itself must be made holy.
36.explain:
“And you shall offer a bull every day as a sin offering for atonement.”

A sin offering is made “every day” of the seven.

“You shall cleanse the altar when you make atonement for it, and you shall anoint it to sanctify it.”

The altar itself must be cleansed, atoned for, and anointed. Even the place of sacrifice must be made holy.

37.brief: For seven days atonement is made for the altar and it is sanctified, and it becomes most holy, so that “Whatever touches the altar must be holy.” The altar is set apart as most holy, and whatever touches it must itself be holy.
37.explain:
“Seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and sanctify it.”

Atonement is made for the altar all seven days.

“And the altar shall be most holy. Whatever touches the altar must be holy.”

The altar becomes “most holy.” Whatever touches it must itself be holy. The altar is set apart as most holy, and whatever touches it must be holy.
37.notes: The Hebrew of the last clause can be read either as whatever touches the altar must be holy, or as whatever touches the altar becomes holy. Haggai 2:11–13 shows that holiness is not passed by contact the way uncleanness is.

38.brief: Two lambs of the first year are to be offered on the altar every day continually. The altar’s ongoing purpose is daily worship.
38.explain:
“Now this is what you shall offer on the altar: two lambs of the first year, day by day continually.”

The altar’s ongoing purpose is daily worship. “Two lambs” are offered “day by day continually.”

39.brief: One lamb is offered in the morning and the other at twilight. Israel’s days begin and end with sacrifice.
39.explain:
“One lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight.”

One lamb in “the morning” and one “at twilight.” Israel’s days begin and end with sacrifice.
39.notes: Acts 3:1 mentions the ninth hour, the time of the evening sacrifice, as “the hour of prayer.” Psalm 141:2 links evening prayer with the evening sacrifice.

40.brief: With the morning lamb come a tenth of an ephah of flour mixed with oil and a fourth of a hin of wine as a drink offering. Grain and wine accompany the daily offering.
40.explain:
“With the one lamb shall be one-tenth of an ephah of flour mixed with one-fourth of a hin of pressed oil,”

A grain offering of flour mixed with oil accompanies the lamb.

“and one-fourth of a hin of wine as a drink offering.”

Wine is poured out as “a drink offering.” Grain and wine accompany the daily offering.
40.notes: A hin was a liquid measure, perhaps about a gallon.

41.brief: The evening lamb is offered with the same grain and drink offerings, “for a sweet aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.” Evening worship matches the morning.
41.explain:
“And the other lamb you shall offer at twilight;”

The evening lamb follows the same pattern.

“and you shall offer with it the grain offering and the drink offering, as in the morning, for a sweet aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.”

Evening worship matches the morning.

42.brief: The offering is to be “a continual burnt offering throughout your generations” at the door of the tabernacle, “where I will meet you to speak with you.” There the LORD promises to meet Moses and speak with him, at the entrance where the daily offering is made.
42.explain:
“This shall be a continual burnt offering throughout your generations at the door of the tabernacle of meeting before the LORD,”

The daily offering will continue “throughout your generations.”

“where I will meet you to speak with you.”

At the entrance, where the offering burns, God promises to meet and speak. The daily sacrifice is connected with God’s meeting and speaking with His people.

43.brief: “And there I will meet with the children of Israel, and the tabernacle shall be sanctified by My glory.” God’s own glory will make the place holy.
43.explain:
“And there I will meet with the children of Israel,”

God will meet not only with Moses but with the whole people.

“and the tabernacle shall be sanctified by My glory.”

God’s “glory” will make the tabernacle holy. The place is holy because God is there (40:34–35).

44.brief: God will consecrate the tabernacle, the altar, and Aaron and his sons to minister as priests. God Himself is the One who makes them holy.
44.explain:
“So I will consecrate the tabernacle of meeting and the altar.”

God Himself will “consecrate” the tent and the altar.

“I will also consecrate both Aaron and his sons to minister to Me as priests.”

The rituals Moses performs are the means. God Himself is the One who makes them holy.

45.brief: “I will dwell among the children of Israel and will be their God.” God states the heart of His purpose: to live among His people.
45.explain:
“I will dwell among the children of Israel and will be their God.”

This is the heart of God’s purpose: to live among His people and to be their God (compare 6:7; Leviticus 26:11–12). The promise reaches its fulfillment when God dwells with His people forever (Revelation 21:3). Paul applies this promise to the church, quoting God’s words, “I will dwell in them” (2 Corinthians 6:16).

46.brief: Israel will know that He is the LORD their God, “who brought them up out of the land of Egypt, that I may dwell among them.” God declares that He rescued Israel from Egypt in order to dwell with them, the stated goal of the whole book.
46.explain:
“And they shall know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them up out of the land of Egypt, that I may dwell among them.”

God states why He brought Israel out of Egypt. He did it “that I may dwell among them.” The exodus was not only rescue from slavery. It was rescue for fellowship with God.

“I am the LORD their God.”

The chapter ends with God’s name. The sanctuary is God’s provision for His presence among the people He redeemed.
